Hardness of Identification. Since we have introduced a new model that is limiting the power of the adversary, it is worth understanding how restrictive this change is. Towards that end, we study how the landscape of identification changes under our definition. Our result below shows that, even for simple collections of languages, identification remains intractable for any M > 1. We leave a full characterization of identification for M -bounded adversaries as an interesting open question. Theorem 37 There is a countable collection L for which no algorithm can identify in the limit, even when restricted to M -bounded enumerations for any M > 1. Proof Let L = {N} ∪ {N \ {n} : n ∈ N} be the collection consisting of the natural numbers and all its subsets obtained by deleting a single number. Let A be any algorithm. The adversary begins by enumerating the natural numbers 1, 2, . . . . If A never outputs N, we are done. Let n1 be the first step when A outputs N. Then at step n1 + 1, we output n1 + 2 instead of n1 +1 and then continue enumerating the natural numbers in the canonical order. If A never outputs N \ {n1 + 1}, we are done. Otherwise, let n2 > n1 be the first step when A outputs N \ {n1 + 1}. At step n2 + 1, the adversary “fills in” the previously skipped element by outputting n1 + 1, instead of n2 + 1, and then continues enumerating the natural numbers in the canonical order again. Repeat. All in all, the adversary can always ensure that A does not correctly identify after any finite time. On the other hand, if we let σ(n) denote the value of the element the adversary enumerates at step n, then σ(n) ≤ n + 1. Thus identification in the limit remains impossible in general even under M -bounded displacement enumerations, for any M > 1.
